title: Hidden-Gem Wine Areas
quiz.0.question: What geographical feature does "Alto" in Alto Piemonte reflect?
quiz.0.options.0: Its northerly latitude — Italy's northernmost wine area
quiz.0.options.1: Higher ground: the hills of northern Piemonte near the Alpine foothills of Monte Rosa
quiz.0.options.2: A high plateau, higher than Barolo and Barbaresco
quiz.0.options.3: "Alto" is a historic place name unrelated to elevation
quiz.0.explanation: Alto Piemonte (northern Piemonte) lies in the north of the region near the Alpine foothills of Monte Rosa. The climate is cooler, and the soils are mostly acidic volcanic porphyry, glacial moraine and marine sands — quite unlike the calcareous marl of Barolo/Barbaresco to the south — giving Nebbiolo a completely different style here.
quiz.1.question: What are the "Carema stone pillars" of Carema DOC?
quiz.1.options.1: Granite pillars supporting pergolas for the vines, locally called "Pilun", with both farming and cultural-landscape value
quiz.1.options.2: A modern art installation to attract tourists
quiz.1.options.3: Pillars in the stone cellars where casks are aged
quiz.1.explanation: Carema's traditional training system uses granite pillars (locally "Pilun") to support pergolas for the vines — the pillars absorb the sun's heat by day and release it slowly at night, helping the grapes ripen fully in the cold Alpine foothills. The system is both farming wisdom and Carema's most iconic cultural landscape.
quiz.2.question: What are Gattinara DOCG and Ghemme DOCG known as?
quiz.2.explanation: Gattinara DOCG and Ghemme DOCG are known as "Alto Piemonte's twin DOCGs" — facing each other across the Sesia river, both are built on Nebbiolo (locally Spanna) and are Alto Piemonte's highest DOCG classification, yet they lag far behind Barolo/Barbaresco in fame, making them favourites of advanced enthusiasts and shrewd collectors.
quiz.3.question: What is the significance of Nervi-Conterno for Alto Piemonte?
quiz.3.options.0: It is Alto Piemonte's oldest estate, founded in 1906
quiz.3.options.1: Roberto Conterno of Giacomo Conterno (Barolo's most legendary estate) bought Nervi in 2018, bringing enormous attention
quiz.3.options.2: Nervi and Conterno are two competing Gattinara estates
quiz.3.options.3: Nervi-Conterno is the name of Alto Piemonte's wine consortium
quiz.3.explanation: In 2018 Roberto Conterno, heir to Barolo's most legendary estate Giacomo Conterno, bought Nervi, Gattinara's oldest-established estate. It drew intense international media attention and prompted the fine-wine market to reassess all of Alto Piemonte.
quiz.4.question: Why is Lessona DOC Alto Piemonte's most mysterious area?
quiz.4.options.0: Because it is a secret estate closed to visitors
quiz.4.options.1: Because it is tiny (around ten hectares) with very small production, and very hard to find on international markets
quiz.4.options.2: Because its wines are not sold, only kept for private collections
quiz.4.options.3: Because its style is completely different from every other Italian wine
quiz.4.explanation: Lessona DOC is tiny (around ten hectares), one of Italy's smallest DOCs, with very limited production. The wines of its key producers, Proprietà Sperino and Sella, are very hard to find on international markets, making it Alto Piemonte's most mysterious area.
quiz.5.question: What is special about the Le Piane estate in Boca DOC?
quiz.5.options.0: It is the largest estate in Boca DOC
quiz.5.options.1: The Swiss Christoph Künzli came to Boca and founded Le Piane, almost single-handedly bringing Boca DOC back into the international spotlight
quiz.5.options.2: Le Piane is Boca's oldest historic estate, founded in the 15th century
quiz.5.options.3: Le Piane was Italy's first certified-organic DOCG estate
quiz.5.explanation: The Swiss Christoph Künzli has made wine in Boca since 1998, taking over old vines and founding Le Piane, and almost single-handedly brought the nearly vanished Boca DOC back into view on the international fine-wine market. His flagship Boca (mainly Nebbiolo with Vespolina) has become the area's benchmark.
quiz.6.question: Compared with Barolo/Barbaresco, what is Alto Piemonte's greatest appeal for collectors?
quiz.6.options.0: Alto Piemonte's wine quality is far higher than Barolo's
quiz.6.options.1: Prices are still clearly lower than Barolo/Barbaresco, yet the wines are also made from Nebbiolo with long ageing potential — an "undervalued" area
quiz.6.options.2: Alto Piemonte wines mature faster, with no need to wait
quiz.6.options.3: Government subsidies in Alto Piemonte keep prices stable
quiz.6.explanation: Top Alto Piemonte wines (Gattinara Riserva, Boca Le Piane and others) cost clearly less than Barolo Riserva of a similar level, with similar ageing potential (15-25 years). Nervi-Conterno's arrival sent the market a strong signal, making it an undervalued area in the eyes of shrewd collectors; but secondary-market liquidity is lower, so treat these wines as for drinking as much as collecting.
slides.0.title: Hidden-Gem Wine Areas
slides.0.subtitle: Carema · Gattinara · Ghemme · Boca · Lessona — the fine small areas of Alto Piemonte, overshadowed by Barolo
slides.1.title: Alto Piemonte — Forgotten Northern Piemonte
slides.1.content:
Why Was Alto Piemonte Forgotten?

Alto Piemonte (northern Piemonte) was one of the best-known Italian wine areas of the 19th century — Gattinara's reputation in the 1800s was reportedly no lower than Barolo's. But phylloxera, two world wars and post-war industrialisation (the textile industry) drained the countryside of people; vineyards were abandoned on a large scale, shrinking from tens of thousands of hectares in the 19th century to only around a thousand today. Now this almost-forgotten land is drawing the attention of collectors worldwide again, thanks to a few dedicated growers and the arrival of fine-wine names such as Nervi-Conterno.

Location: northern Piemonte, in the Alpine foothills of Monte Rosa | Climate: continental, cooler than the Langhe | Soils: volcanic porphyry, glacial moraine, marine sands (mostly acidic)

The Fundamental Differences from Barolo/Barbaresco

Soils: Barolo/Barbaresco sit on calcareous marl (alkaline); Alto Piemonte has volcanic porphyry, glacial moraine and marine sands (acidic) — with the same Nebbiolo, acidic soils give higher acidity, finer tannins and more pronounced minerality, in a style closer to Burgundy
Elevation: Alto Piemonte's vineyards lie at 300-700 m, generally higher than the Langhe hills, with larger day-night swings and a longer growing season, which helps retain acidity and aromatic complexity
Blends: Alto Piemonte's Nebbiolo (locally called "Spanna") is usually blended with Vespolina (spicy) and Uva Rara (locally called Bonarda, round fruit) as well as Croatina; the rules allow each DOC/DOCG different proportions of other grapes
slides.2.title: Carema DOC — The Stone-Pillar Pergolas of the Alpine Foothills
slides.2.content:
Nebbiolo on Stone Pillars

Carema is one of Italy's most extreme wine areas — on the border with Valle d'Aosta at 350-600 m, it is one of Nebbiolo's northernmost limits. Growers built terraces on steep moraine slopes and traditional stone-pillar pergolas (Pilun); the pillars absorb the sun's heat by day and release it at night, helping grapes ripen in such a cold setting. Production is tiny, making it one of the smallest DOCs in Italy.

DOC (1967) | Elevation: 350-600 m | Soils: glacial moraine, granitic acidic soils | Production: tiny

Carema: Grape Character and Producers

Rules: at least 85% Nebbiolo (locally Picotener); minimum ageing 2 years (Riserva 3 years)
Style: lighter and more refined than Barolo; red berries (strawberry, raspberry) + rose + high acidity + minerality; ages 10-20 years
Top producer: Luigi Ferrando (Black Label / White Label, made in tiny amounts; Carema's most legendary estate)
Cantina dei Produttori Nebbiolo di Carema: a co-operative (founded 1960) that brings together the old vines of many small growers; Carema's largest producer, with an easier-drinking style and excellent value
slides.3.title: Gattinara DOCG & Ghemme DOCG — The Twin DOCGs
slides.3.content:
Gattinara DOCG — Once Barolo's Equal

History: in the 19th century Gattinara was famous across Europe, its reputation reportedly no lower than Barolo's. DOC in 1967 and DOCG in 1990, it was Alto Piemonte's first DOCG; its soils are acidic volcanic porphyry left by an ancient supervolcano
Rules: at least 90% Nebbiolo (Spanna), with small amounts of Vespolina (up to 4%) and Uva Rara (Bonarda) allowed; minimum ageing 35 months (Riserva 47 months)
Top producers: Nervi-Conterno (Vigna Valferana, Vigna Molsino), Antoniolo (Osso San Grato, San Francesco single vineyards), Travaglini (Tre Vigne)

Ghemme DOCG — Gattinara's Sister DOCG

Standing: facing Gattinara across the Sesia river (on its east bank, in the province of Novara), it became a DOCG in 1997 — Alto Piemonte's second — and the two are known as the "twin DOCGs"; soils are mainly glacial moraine
Rules: at least 85% Nebbiolo (Spanna), with Vespolina and/or Uva Rara up to 15%; minimum ageing 34 months (Riserva 46 months)
Style difference: Ghemme can use more Vespolina (spice) and Uva Rara (roundness), so it is generally softer and easier to drink than Gattinara — the "approachable version" of Alto Piemonte
Top producers: Cantalupo (Collis Breclemae, Signore di Bayard), Torraccia del Piantavigna
slides.4.title: Nervi-Conterno — The Deal That Changed Alto Piemonte's Fate
slides.4.content:
2018: One of the Most Watched Acquisitions in Italian Wine

In 2018 Roberto Conterno, head of Barolo's most legendary estate — Giacomo Conterno (flagship Monfortino) — bought Nervi (founded 1906), Gattinara's most historic estate. The deal not only gave Nervi the Conterno family's winemaking philosophy and international brand power, but also led the global fine-wine market to reassess all of Alto Piemonte — "if Barolo's very best winemaker believes in Gattinara, there must be something here we have overlooked".

Nervi (1906) + Conterno (Monfortino) = Alto Piemonte's strongest signal

Nervi-Conterno Flagship Wines

Gattinara Vigna Valferana: Nervi's historic single vineyard Valferana, old vines on volcanic porphyry. After taking over, Roberto Conterno restored the vineyards and brought more precise winemaking (long maceration, ageing in large oak casks); quality has risen across the board, winning strong praise from international critics
Gattinara Vigna Molsino: another single vineyard, Molsino, also on acidic volcanic soils, more mineral and refined than Valferana and suited to long ageing of 20+ years
Market impact: since the Nervi-Conterno wines were released, the international visibility of Gattinara and all of Alto Piemonte has risen markedly, and other estates such as Antoniolo and Travaglini have also drawn more attention
slides.5.title: Boca DOC & Lessona DOC — The Rarest of the Rare
slides.5.content:
Boca DOC — A Revived Area

Novara hills | DOC (1969)

Historic low: almost entirely abandoned in the 1990s, with only a handful of vineyards and producers left
Hero of the revival: the Swiss Christoph Künzli (Le Piane, making wine in Boca since 1998) took over the old vines of veteran grower Antonio Cerri and almost single-handedly brought Boca DOC back into the international spotlight
Le Piane wines: the flagship Boca (mainly Nebbiolo with Vespolina), plus the Croatina-based Piane and others
Rules and character: Nebbiolo 70-90%, the rest Vespolina and/or Uva Rara; volcanic porphyry soils, and Vespolina's spice (white pepper, clove) is Boca's distinctive flavour signature

Lessona DOC — The Most Mysterious Micro-DOC

Biella hills | DOC (1976)

Extremely scarce: tiny in size (around ten hectares), one of Italy's smallest DOCs
Soils: acidic yellow marine sands left by an ancient sea, giving Nebbiolo delicate aromas and a savoury, saline touch
Rules: at least 85% Nebbiolo (Spanna), the rest may be Vespolina and Uva Rara; Riserva requires longer ageing
Top producers: Proprietà Sperino (the De Marchi family's Lessona estate), Sella (founded 1671, one of Italy's oldest wine families)
Why mysterious: production is tiny, and the wines are very hard to find on international markets

Bramaterra DOC — The Most Balanced Hidden Gem

Biella / Vercelli hills | DOC (1979)

Rules: Nebbiolo 50-80%, Croatina up to 30%, Vespolina and Uva Rara together up to 20% | Riserva requires longer ageing
Style: one of Alto Piemonte's most complex blends; on volcanic porphyry the three grapes combine Nebbiolo's structure with Croatina's fruit and Vespolina's spice — the most "drinkable" Alto Piemonte
Top names: Sella (Bramaterra), Colombera e Garella

Alto Piemonte's Small DOCs at a Glance

Sizzano DOC: Nebbiolo 50-70%, Vespolina, Uva Rara; one of the easiest-drinking DOCs of the Novara hills
Fara DOC: Nebbiolo 50-70%, Vespolina, Uva Rara; tiny volumes, sold almost only locally
Coste della Sesia DOC / Colline Novaresi DOC: regional DOCs covering the west and east banks of the Sesia river respectively — the easiest way in
slides.6.title: Alto Piemonte's Value Logic — Why It Deserves Attention
slides.6.content:
As prices of top Barolo and Barbaresco keep climbing, Alto Piemonte — also made from Nebbiolo and also capable of long ageing — remains a relatively undervalued corner of the Italian fine-wine market.

📊 The Gap Between Quality and Price

Barolo Riserva (top): an established international name and collectors' market, with high prices for top wines | ageing potential: 20-30 years
Gattinara Riserva (top): an equally serious style at clearly lower prices | ageing potential: 15-25 years
Boca, Lessona, Bramaterra: tiny production, strong personalities, prices still relatively accessible | ageing potential: 10-20 years
Conclusion: Alto Piemonte's top wines offer a close quality experience and similar ageing potential at clearly lower prices

🚀 Recent Signs of Attention

The arrival of Nervi-Conterno (2018) made international collectors look at Gattinara again, and other estates such as Antoniolo have benefited too
International wine media have greatly increased their coverage of Alto Piemonte in recent years, and top wines regularly earn high praise
A new generation and returning producers such as Le Piane, Proprietà Sperino and Colombera e Garella have raised quality across the area

⚠️ Notes for Collectors

Liquidity: Alto Piemonte trades far less than Barolo on the secondary market, so wines are not easy to resell
Stability: some small DOCs (Boca, Lessona) have very few producers, and a change of ownership or a closure can affect supply
Suggested approach: treat it as "for drinking as much as collecting" — choose reputable producers and single vineyards, wait patiently for ageing, and enjoy the drinking value of an undervalued area
slides.7.title: Alto Piemonte's Six DOC/DOCGs: A Complete Guide
slides.7.content:
Gattinara DOCG

Nebbiolo 90%+ | minimum ageing 35 months

Alto Piemonte's best-known area / volcanic porphyry soils / revolutionised by Nervi-Conterno / the collector's first choice

Ghemme DOCG

Nebbiolo 85%+ / Vespolina, Uva Rara up to 15%

Gattinara's sister DOCG / glacial moraine / rounder and easier to drink / Cantalupo is the benchmark

Carema DOC

Nebbiolo 85%+ | stone-pillar pergolas (Pilun)

Extreme Nebbiolo on the Alpine border / Luigi Ferrando Black Label / tiny production / great-value co-operative

Boca / Lessona / Bramaterra

Each with its own blending rules

Boca: revived by Le Piane / Lessona: micro-DOC on marine sands / Bramaterra: the most balanced three-grape blend
slides.8.title: Key Takeaways
slides.8.points.0: Alto Piemonte: northern Piemonte near Monte Rosa, on acidic volcanic porphyry, glacial moraine and marine sands (vs the Langhe's calcareous marl); Nebbiolo (locally Spanna) is more refined and mineral, usually blended with Vespolina and Uva Rara (Bonarda)
slides.8.points.1: Carema DOC: one of Nebbiolo's northernmost limits, with its stone-pillar pergolas (Pilun) as a cultural landscape; Luigi Ferrando Black Label is the benchmark; production is tiny
slides.8.points.2: Gattinara DOCG (1990): Alto Piemonte's first DOCG, its 19th-century reputation reportedly no lower than Barolo's; the Nervi-Conterno acquisition (2018) sparked market attention
slides.8.points.3: Nervi-Conterno: Roberto Conterno (of Barolo Monfortino fame) bought Nervi in 2018; flagship single vineyards Vigna Valferana + Vigna Molsino; it drew international attention to all of Gattinara and Alto Piemonte
slides.8.points.4: Ghemme DOCG (1997): Gattinara's "sister DOCG", may use more Vespolina and Uva Rara, rounder in style; Cantalupo is the benchmark
slides.8.points.5: Boca DOC: the Swiss Christoph Künzli (Le Piane) revived this nearly abandoned area from 1998; Vespolina's white-pepper spice is its signature
slides.8.points.6: Lessona DOC: one of Italy's smallest DOCs, on acidic marine sands; Proprietà Sperino + Sella (1671!) are the leading producers
slides.8.points.7: Value logic: top Alto Piemonte wines such as Gattinara cost clearly less than Barolo Riserva with similar ageing potential; but secondary-market liquidity is low, so treat them as for drinking as much as collecting
slides.9.title: Hidden-Gem Areas Knowledge Check
slides.9.questions.0.question: What is the function of Carema DOC's granite-pillar pergolas (Pilun)?
slides.9.questions.0.options.0: Purely decorative, with no practical function
slides.9.questions.0.options.1: They absorb the sun's heat by day and release it slowly at night, helping grapes ripen in a cold setting
slides.9.questions.0.explanation: Carema's granite pillars (Pilun) absorb a great deal of the sun's heat by day and release it slowly at night, helping grapes ripen fully in the cold climate of the Alpine border. They are a perfect union of farming wisdom and cultural landscape.
slides.9.questions.1.question: What is the main stylistic difference between Gattinara DOCG and Ghemme DOCG?
slides.9.questions.1.options.1: Gattinara has more Nebbiolo (90%+) and a stronger structure; Ghemme may use more Vespolina and Uva Rara, rounder and easier to drink
slides.9.questions.1.options.2: The two are almost identical in style
slides.9.questions.1.options.3: Ghemme has greater ageing potential than Gattinara
slides.9.questions.1.explanation: Gattinara requires at least 90% Nebbiolo, giving a stronger, more refined structure; Ghemme allows up to 15% Vespolina and Uva Rara, with more pronounced spice and an overall rounder style — the "approachable version" of Alto Piemonte.
slides.9.questions.2.question: What is the background to the founding of Nervi-Conterno?
slides.9.questions.2.options.0: A brand-new estate founded in Gattinara by a newcomer
slides.9.questions.2.options.1: Roberto Conterno (Barolo Monfortino) bought the historic Nervi estate in 2018, sparking an international reassessment of Alto Piemonte
slides.9.questions.2.options.2: A co-operative estate backed by an Italian government subsidy scheme
slides.9.questions.2.options.3: A joint brand created by a marriage between the Nervi and Conterno families
slides.9.questions.2.explanation: In 2018 Roberto Conterno, head of Barolo's most legendary estate Giacomo Conterno, bought the historic Gattinara estate Nervi (1906), renaming it Nervi-Conterno, which prompted the global fine-wine market to reassess all of Alto Piemonte.
slides.9.questions.3.question: What is the special story of the Le Piane estate in Boca DOC?
slides.9.questions.3.options.0: It is Boca's oldest noble estate, founded in the 1600s
slides.9.questions.3.options.1: The Swiss Christoph Künzli has made wine in Boca since 1998, almost single-handedly reviving the nearly abandoned Boca DOC
slides.9.questions.3.options.2: It is the second label of the Antoniolo family
slides.9.questions.3.options.3: It was Italy's first certified-organic DOC estate
slides.9.questions.3.explanation: From 1998 the Swiss Christoph Künzli took over old vines in Boca and founded Le Piane, almost single-handedly bringing the nearly vanished Boca DOC back to the international fine-wine market; his Boca is the area's benchmark.
slides.9.questions.4.question: Why is Lessona DOC "Alto Piemonte's most mysterious area"?
slides.9.questions.4.options.0: Because it does not sell its wine at all
slides.9.questions.4.options.1: It is tiny (around ten hectares) with very small production, and very hard to find on international markets
slides.9.questions.4.options.2: Because its location cannot be seen on a map
slides.9.questions.4.options.3: Because its production methods are secret
slides.9.questions.4.explanation: Lessona DOC is tiny (around ten hectares), one of Italy's smallest DOCs, with very small production that is very hard to find on international markets, making it Alto Piemonte's hardest-to-find rare area.
slides.9.questions.5.question: What is the fundamental difference between the soils of Alto Piemonte and the Langhe (Barolo/Barbaresco)?
slides.9.questions.5.options.0: The Langhe is granite, Alto Piemonte limestone
slides.9.questions.5.options.1: Alto Piemonte has mostly acidic soils (volcanic porphyry, glacial moraine, marine sands), the Langhe calcareous marl — giving the same Nebbiolo quite different styles
slides.9.questions.5.options.2: The soils are exactly the same
slides.9.questions.5.options.3: Alto Piemonte is sand, the Langhe clay
slides.9.questions.5.explanation: Alto Piemonte's acidic soils (volcanic porphyry, glacial moraine, marine sands) versus the Langhe's calcareous marl are the most fundamental difference, giving the same Nebbiolo a quite different style — higher acidity, finer tannins and more pronounced minerality, closer to Burgundy.
slides.9.questions.6.question: What is Alto Piemonte's core appeal for collectors?
slides.9.questions.6.options.0: Quality far higher than Barolo, not yet recognised by the market
slides.9.questions.6.options.1: Top wines cost clearly less than Barolo, with similar ageing potential — an undervalued area
slides.9.questions.6.options.2: The Italian government offers investment subsidies
slides.9.questions.6.options.3: It produces more than Barolo and is easier to obtain
slides.9.questions.6.explanation: Top Alto Piemonte wines such as Gattinara Riserva cost clearly less than Barolo Riserva of similar quality, yet have similar ageing potential (15-25 years). Nervi-Conterno's arrival sent a strong market signal, making it an undervalued area in the eyes of shrewd collectors.
